page: Microsoft Azure E64s_v5 is an ESv5-series virtual machine configured with 64 vCPUs and 512.0 GB of RAM, yielding an 8.0 GB memory-to-vCPU ratio. Powered by an Intel Xeon 8370C processor running at 2.8 GHz, this x86_64 architecture server features 32 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The CPU cache configuration includes 48 KB of L1d cache, 1 MB of L2 cache, and 48 MB of L3 cache. This instance does not include local storage or GPUs, relying instead on external Premium Storage.

Benchmark data indicates strong multi-core performance, with stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and Passmark CPU scores all placing in the top 25%. Memory performance is also robust, with uncached large-block read and write bandwidth tests scoring in the top 25%, alongside strong Passmark memory and database operation results. However, single-core performance remains in the average tier, as shown by stress-ng and Geekbench single-core benchmarks.

While the instance excels in multi-threaded tasks, such as bzip3 multi-threaded decompression and static web serving throughput, it exhibits limitations in heavy computational tasks like large-scale LLM inference. Specifically, text generation using a large 70B model falls into the bottom 25% performance tier. Given the high memory density and strong database operation benchmarks, this instance is well-suited for memory-intensive workloads, including relational databases, in-memory caching systems like Redis, and multi-threaded enterprise applications.
description: Microsoft Azure E64s_v5 is a memory-optimized virtual machine featuring 64 vCPUs and 512.0 GB of RAM, powered by an Intel Xeon 8370C processor at 2.8 GHz. Built on the x86_64 architecture with 32 physical cores, it utilizes Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. The instance lacks local storage and GPUs, relying on external Premium Storage. Performance benchmarks show strong multi-core CPU capabilities and high memory bandwidth, placing in the top 25% for multi-threaded decompression, database operations, and Redis SET operations. However, single-core performance is average, and large-scale LLM text generation is a notable bottleneck, scoring in the bottom 25% for 70B models. This configuration is highly efficient for memory-intensive enterprise applications, relational databases, and caching layers.
